result.summary: Circe questions Medea and Jason, learns of the murder of Apsyrtus, and sends them away unpurified in anger. Hera sends Iris and Thetis to help, and the Nereids guide the Argo past the Sirens, Scylla, Charybdis and the Wandering rocks. The Argonauts reach the Phaeacians, where Medea begs Arete and the heroes for protection from the pursuing Colchians.

scenes.title: Circe questions the suppliants
scenes.summary: Circe asks about their journey, Medea tells all but the murder of Apsyrtus, and Circe sees through her. She condemns the deed and sends them from her halls.
scenes.stakes: Medea needs Circe's mercy and is in danger of rejection and her father's wrath.

scenes.title: Hera enlists Thetis
scenes.summary: Hera sends Iris to Thetis, Hephaestus and Aeolus. She asks Thetis to help the Argo, recalling Thetis's marriage to Peleus. Thetis agrees and gathers the Nereids.
scenes.stakes: The Argonauts face destruction at the rocks, Scylla and Charybdis without divine help.

scenes.title: Thetis speaks to Peleus
scenes.summary: Thetis secretly tells Peleus to sail at dawn. The text recalls how she left him after he saw her burning Achilles to make him immortal.
scenes.stakes: Peleus risks angering Thetis again if he reveals her.

scenes.title: The Sirens
scenes.summary: The Argo sails past Anthemoessa. Orpheus' lyre overpowers the Sirens' song, but Butes leaps overboard and is saved by Cypris.
scenes.stakes: The crew risk being lured to death by the Sirens' song.

scenes.title: Through the Wandering rocks
scenes.summary: The Nereids toss the Argo between the rocks while Hera and Hephaestus watch. The ship then passes the cattle of Helios on Thrinacia.
scenes.stakes: The ship could be smashed by the rocks, Scylla and Charybdis.

scenes.title: Medea pleads at Drepane
scenes.summary: The Argonauts are welcomed by Alcinous, but a Colchian host arrives demanding Medea. She begs Arete and the heroes, who swear to protect her, and she lies sleepless.
scenes.stakes: Medea may be handed back to Aeetes and killed.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet by which Hecate is called as Scylla's mother.

notable_quotes.reason: Hera's aphorism that even gods suffer blindness of folly.
Memorable simile of the Nereids tossing the ship like a ball.

analysis.text: Medea's guilt over Apsyrtus' murder meets Circe's refusal to purify her, while divine help guides the heroes home.
The route through the western Mediterranean reflects Greek geographic lore about Italy and Sicily, also seen in Homer's Odyssey.

legacy.text: Apollonius' Wandering rocks and Sirens episodes draw on Homer's Odyssey and shaped later retellings of the Argonaut voyage.

fun_facts.text: Apollonius of Rhodes wrote in the 3rd century BC, and the Argonautica is the only complete surviving Hellenistic epic.

language_notes.text: Circe and Aeetes are children of Helios the sun, so the golden gleam from their eyes marks Medea as kin.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose".
"The hero" here is Jason, who leads Medea out.
"Hie thee" means hurry; "pinions" are wings.
The Wandering rocks are the clashing, fire-lashed rocks the Argo passed earlier with Hera's help.
Themis revealed the prophecy that Thetis's son would be greater than his father, so Zeus gave up pursuing her.
Thetis's son is Achilles, raised by the centaur Cheiron. Elysian plain is the paradise of the blessed dead, where he will wed Medea.
Ausonian means Italian; Phoreys is a sea-god, father of Scylla in this account.
Peleus, son of Aeaeus, was Thetis' mortal husband; their son was Achilles. The sea-goddess is invisible to the others, as gods often are in epic.
The Planctae, 'Wandering Rocks', were clashing or drifting rocks that endangered ships; the Nereids (sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus) will guide the Argo through.
'Thou' and 'ye' are archaic forms: 'ye' is plural (the crew), 'thou' singular (Peleus alone). 'Meet time' means to meet the ship.
Ambrosia, the food of the gods, with fire was meant to burn away Achilles' mortal part and make him immortal.
Thwarts are the rowers' benches across the ship; sheets are ropes controlling the sail.
The Sirens once attended Persephone (Demeter's daughter), who was carried off to the underworld; their bird-like form is often explained as a result of that loss.
Bistonian means Thracian, from the Bistones, a Thracian people; Orpheus was a Thracian singer.
Scylla and Charybdis are the sea-monster and whirlpool flanking a narrow strait; sailors passing one risked the other. Here they mark the perilous route's end.
Hephaestus, god of the forge, is linked to volcanic fire; the lingering vapour implies his smithy-fires once burned beneath these rocks.
Compares the length of the toil to a long spring day: the ordeal lasted as long as daylight stretches in spring.
Kine means cattle; mead means meadow. Both are archaic words.
Orichalcum is a precious golden-looking metal of ancient legend, often prized like bronze or gold.
The sickle is the one Cronos used to castrate his father Uranus. The poet apologizes because the tale is an unpleasant one to tell.
Drepane means 'sickle' in Greek, which is why the island's name follows from the story of the sickle or reaping-hook.
'Thou wouldst say' is a poet's address to the reader, inviting them to imagine the scene as an observer.
Haemonia is an old name for Thessaly, the homeland of Jason and the Argonauts.
The 'maiden that wanders by night, daughter of Perses' is Hecate, Medea's patron goddess of witchcraft, invoked as a witness to her oath.
'Raft' is an archaic past form of 'reave', meaning taken away by force.
The Fury that avenges suppliants reflects the Greek belief that gods punish those who harm people seeking protection.

context_notes.text: Suppliants sat at a host's hearth to claim protection, a sacred custom of hospitality.
Medea has just helped murder her brother Apsyrtus; she hides this because it makes her guilty of kin-slaying, which Circe has come to purify.
Hephaestus is the smith god, whose forge fires and hammering would endanger passing ships.
Aeolus keeps and controls the winds.
Thetis is a sea-goddess raised by Hera, whom Zeus desired.
Hera favours the Argonauts and Jason, and directs their journey home through the divine help of Thetis and the Nereids.
The Sirens lure sailors with irresistible song and then kill them; Achelous is a river god, their father.
Cypris is Aphrodite, named for Cyprus; Eryx in Sicily had a famous temple of hers. Lilybaeum is in western Sicily.
Thetis, a sea-goddess and chief of the Nereids (sea-nymphs, daughters of Nereus), helps the Argo because Hera asked her to protect the heroes.
The 'spouse of Zeus' is Hera, the Argonauts' divine patron; Athena is her companion in aiding the expedition.
Thrinacia is the island where the sacred cattle of Helios, the sun god, graze; in the Odyssey Ulysses' men are doomed for slaughtering them.
The Phaeacians were said to descend from Uranus, the sky god, through the blood shed when Cronos mutilated him.
Touching the knees was the formal gesture of a suppliant, placing oneself under the protection of the person addressed.
Medea stresses her virginity because it bears on her claim that she fled out of fear, not desire, and on how Alcinous might judge her.

literary_notes.text: Circe's pity mixed with blunt condemnation shows her as perceptive, stern and bound by kinship.
Hera's brief general saying excuses Zeus's folly and softens Thetis's lingering anger to win her help.
The hair's breadth escape conveys how narrow the heroes' safety will be.
Thetis' speed is compared to a flash of the eye and sunbeams, stressing her divine swiftness.
Thetis is likened to a breath of wind and a dream, conveying how swiftly and insubstantially she vanishes.
The 'lily-like voice' fuses sound with delicate beauty, making the deadly song seem lovely and pure.
Orpheus' music defeats the Sirens' song, showing art overpowering a lure that would otherwise destroy the crew.
Butes' impulsive leap and the narrator's 'poor wretch' show how the Sirens' power overwhelms even a hero's will.
Playful dolphins around a ship turn the Nereids' dangerous work into graceful, joyful movement, easing the tension.
The Nereids tossing the Argo is compared to girls playing ball, making the ship weightless and the danger seem like play.
Hephaestus resting calmly on his hammer while Hera clutches Athena in fear contrasts divine spectators' reactions, highlighting the peril.
The milk-white cattle with golden horns create a bright, serene picture after the smoky danger, marking a shift in mood.
Medea lists what she lost and what she gave, presenting herself as a sacrificing, wronged victim to shame the heroes.
Medea's sudden bitter exclamation turns directly on the heroes, breaking from her pleading into reproach.
Night is given an active role, putting men's labours to rest and lulling the earth, which sharpens the contrast with Medea's wakefulness.
Medea's sleepless grief is compared to a poor widow spinning through the night amid weeping children, a homely image that makes her anguish human.
